SMALL CLAIMS COURT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Riverside Movers LLC

PROPOSED PLAINTIFF — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF A SMALL CLAIMS CASE
I, Jordan Lee, am considering suing Riverside Movers LLC in California small claims court for $1,850, based on: An unpaid refund for a canceled moving service, as itemized in the attached invoice. This declaration provides background information for use alongside an actual small claims filing, most commonly Form SC-100, Plaintiff's Claim and ORDER to Go to Small Claims Court, to be filed with the California superior court for the county of filing: Sacramento County. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and preparing or signing it does not file a claim, serve Riverside Movers LLC, or determine the amount, if any, Riverside Movers LLC owes Jordan Lee. Only an actual court filing, proper service on Riverside Movers LLC, and a judgment following a hearing (or Riverside Movers LLC's default) can do that.

THE SMALL CLAIMS DOLLAR LIMIT
California's small claims court jurisdiction is set by dollar limit. Code of Civil Procedure § 116.220(a)(1) gives the small claims court jurisdiction, except as provided in subdivisions (c), (e), and (f), for recovery of money, if the amount of the demand does not exceed six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($6,250); subdivision (a) also extends that same $6,250 limit to enforcing certain delinquent unsecured personal property taxes the defendant does not contest, to issuing certain writs of possession, to confirming or vacating a fee arbitration award between an attorney and client, and to an injunction or other equitable relief only when a statute expressly authorizes small claims court to award it. Section 116.221 raises this limit for an individual plaintiff: in addition to the jurisdiction conferred by Section 116.220, the small claims court has jurisdiction in an action brought by a natural person if the amount of the demand does not exceed twelve thousand five hundred dollars ($12,500), except as otherwise prohibited by subdivision (c) of Section 116.220 or subdivision (a) of Section 116.231.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "Except as provided in subdivisions (c), (e), and (f), for recovery of money, if the amount of the demand does not exceed six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($6,250)."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.220(a)(1), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.220(a)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.220)
  "In addition to the jurisdiction conferred by Section 116.220, the small claims court has jurisdiction in an action brought by a natural person, if the amount of the demand does not exceed twelve thousand five hundred dollars ($12,500), except as otherwise prohibited by subdivision (c) of Section 116.220 or subdivision (a) of Section 116.231."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.221, Code Civ. Proc. § 116.221 (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.221)

This clause does not describe § 116.220(c)'s separate, lower limit for a claim against a guarantor or an assignee plaintiff -- the text of subdivision (c) itself was not fetched, so nothing is stated about it beyond the fact, which is part of § 116.221's own quoted text, that such an exception exists -- and it does not describe § 116.231(a)'s two-claims-over-$2,500-per-calendar-year filing limit referenced in that same cross-reference; that limit is covered in its own clause, smallclaims_vexatious_filer_limit.

NO ATTORNEY REPRESENTATION AT THE SMALL CLAIMS HEARING
With narrow exceptions, no attorney may take part in the conduct or defense of a small claims action. Code of Civil Procedure § 116.530(a) provides that except as permitted by that section, no attorney may take part in the conduct or defense of a small claims action. Subdivision (b) states this bar does not apply where the attorney appears by or against himself or herself, by or against a partnership in which he or she is a general partner and all the partners are attorneys, or by or against a professional corporation of which he or she is an officer or director and all other officers and directors are attorneys. Subdivision (c) separately provides that nothing in the section prevents an attorney from providing advice to a party to a small claims action, either before or after the action is commenced, from testifying to facts of which the attorney has personal knowledge and about which the attorney is competent to testify, from representing a party in an appeal to the superior court, or from representing a party in connection with the enforcement of a judgment.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]

  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.530(a), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.530(a) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.530)
  "Providing advice to a party to a small claims action, either before or after the commencement of the action."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.530(c)(1), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.530(c)(1) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.530)

  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.530(c)(3)-(4), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.530(c)(3)-(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.530)

This clause does not cover any procedure for how a hearing officer or the court itself addresses a party who shows up with an attorney in violation of subdivision (a); the fetched text states the prohibition and its exceptions but not an enforcement mechanism.

SERVING THE CLAIM ON THE DEFENDANT
Code of Civil Procedure § 116.340(a) allows service of the claim and order on the defendant by the clerk mailing a copy by any form of mail providing for a return receipt, by the plaintiff delivering a copy to the defendant in person, by substituted service as provided in Section 415.20, or by the clerk mailing the claim and issuing and mailing the order as provided in Section 116.330(b). Subdivision (b) sets the deadline: service of the claim and order on the defendant shall be completed at least 15 days before the hearing date if the defendant resides within the county in which the action is filed, or at least 20 days before the hearing date if the defendant resides outside that county. Subdivision (c) requires proof of service of the claim and order to be filed with the small claims court before the hearing.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "The plaintiff may cause a copy of the claim and order to be delivered to the defendant in person."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.340(a)(2), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.340(a)(2) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.340)
  "Service of the claim and order on the defendant shall be completed at least 15 days before the hearing date if the defendant resides within the county in which the action is filed, or at least 20 days before the hearing date if the defendant resides outside the county in which the action is filed."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.340(b), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.340(b) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.340)

This clause's paraphrase of subdivision (c)'s own deadline for filing proof of service is not independently quoted here; only the 15-day/20-day service deadline in subdivision (b) is directly quoted below.

THE DEFENDANT'S CLAIM: SUING BACK IN THE SAME CASE
Code of Civil Procedure § 116.360(a) allows the defendant to file a claim against the plaintiff in the same action, up to the jurisdictional limits stated in Sections 116.220, 116.221, and 116.231; the defendant's claim need not relate to the same subject or event as the plaintiff's claim. Subdivision (b) requires the defendant's claim to be filed and served in the manner provided for the plaintiff's claim under Sections 116.330 and 116.340. Subdivision (c) requires the defendant to serve a copy of the claim and order on the plaintiff at least five days before the hearing date, or, if the defendant was served 10 days or less before the hearing date, at least one day before the hearing date.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "The defendant may file a claim against the plaintiff in the same action in an amount not to exceed the jurisdictional limits stated in Section 116.220, 116.221, and 116.231. The claim need not relate to the same subject or event as the plaintiff’s claim."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.360(a), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.360(a) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.360)
  "The defendant shall cause a copy of the claim and order to be served on the plaintiff at least five days before the hearing date, unless the defendant was served 10 days or less before the hearing date, in which event the defendant shall cause a copy of the defendant’s claim and order to be served on the plaintiff at least one day before the hearing date."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.360(c), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.360(c) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.360)
  Known gap: Verified against the actual text of Code of Civil Procedure § 116.360, fetched from california.public.law -- see smallclaims_jurisdiction_and_dollar_limits's gap note for the sourcing convention. This clause does not independently verify Sections 116.330 or 116.220/116.221/116.231's own text beyond what is already quoted in their own clauses in this document (jurisdiction and service); it relies on § 116.360's own cross-references to them.

THE JUDGMENT, AND THE ASYMMETRIC RIGHT TO APPEAL
Code of Civil Procedure § 116.610(a) requires the small claims court to give judgment for damages, equitable relief, or both, within the jurisdictional limits stated in Sections 116.220, 116.221, and 116.231, and permits the court to make orders as to time of payment or otherwise as it deems just and equitable. Subdivision (b) lets the court continue the matter to permit and encourage informal or alternative resolution. California's appeal right is not symmetric between the parties. Code of Civil Procedure § 116.710(a) provides that the plaintiff in a small claims action has no right to appeal the judgment on the plaintiff's claim, but a plaintiff who did not appear at the hearing may file a motion to vacate the judgment under Section 116.720. Subdivision (b) allows the defendant, with respect to the plaintiff's claim, and the plaintiff, with respect to a claim of the defendant, to appeal the judgment to the superior court in the county where the action was heard. Subdivision (c) allows the defendant's insurer to appeal the judgment on the plaintiff's claim if the judgment exceeds two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) and the insurer stipulates that its policy with the defendant covers the matter. Subdivision (d) provides that a defendant who did not appear at the hearing has no right to appeal the judgment, but may file a motion to vacate the judgment under Section 116.730 or 116.740 and may appeal the denial of that motion.

  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.610(a), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.610(a) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.610)
  "The plaintiff in a small claims action shall have no right to appeal the judgment on the plaintiff’s claim, but a plaintiff who did not appear at the hearing may file a motion to vacate the judgment in accordance with Section 116.720."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.710(a), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.710(a) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.710)

  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.710(b), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.710(b) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.710)
  "the insurer of the defendant may appeal the judgment to the superior court in the county in which the matter was heard if the judgment exceeds two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) and the insurer stipulates that its policy with the defendant covers the matter to which the judgment applies."
  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.710(c), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.710(c) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.710)

This clause does not describe §§ 116.720, 116.730, or 116.740's own procedures and deadlines for a motion to vacate a judgment, or the appellate procedure once an appeal is actually filed (Sections 116.760 et seq.); none of that text was fetched for this clause.

THE LIMIT ON MORE THAN TWO CLAIMS OVER $2,500 IN A CALENDAR YEAR
Code of Civil Procedure § 116.231(a) provides that, except as provided in subdivision (d), no person may file more than two small claims actions in which the amount demanded exceeds two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500), anywhere in the state, in any calendar year. Subdivision (b) requires that if the amount demanded in a small claims action exceeds $2,500, the party making the demand file a declaration under penalty of perjury attesting that not more than two small claims actions with a demand exceeding $2,500 have been filed by that party in the state within the calendar year. Subdivision (d) exempts from the filing limit a city, county, city and county, school district, county office of education, community college district, local district, or other local public entity filing a claim that does not exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000); if such a public entity's small claims action is filed and the defendant notifies the court, in writing in advance or at the hearing, that the defendant is represented by legal counsel, the action is transferred out of the small claims division.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]

  — Code Civ. Proc. § 116.231(d), Code Civ. Proc. § 116.231(d) (https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_116.231)

COLLECTING A SMALL CLAIMS JUDGMENT
Winning a small claims judgment does not, by itself, produce payment. The Judicial Council of California's statewide self-help website states that the court does not collect the money for the winning party, and that collecting can take significant time and money, with no guarantee of collecting any of it. The same page states that a winning party must wait at least 30 days after the Notice of Entry of Judgment was handed or mailed before collecting, and that if the losing party does not pay right away, the losing party must send information about what they own, where they work, and where they bank. The winning party can also ask for a court date (an examination) where the losing party must appear and answer questions about what they earn and own.

  "If the other side won't pay you, the court won't collect it for you"
  — California small claims judgment collection (as described by the Judicial Council of California's Self-Help Center), Judicial Council of California Self-Help Center, "After the Trial" (https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/small-claims/after-trial/if-you-win)

This clause does not describe the specific enforcement mechanisms available (for example, a wage garnishment, a bank levy, or an abstract of judgment recorded against real property), only the general disclosure obligation and examination procedure described on the fetched self-help page.

FREE SMALL CLAIMS ADVISOR SERVICES
California law requires individual small claims advisor assistance in every county. Code of Civil Procedure § 116.260 provides that in each county, individual assistance shall be made available to advise small claims litigants and potential litigants without charge, as provided in Section 116.940 and by rules adopted by the Judicial Council.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]

Neither Section 116.940's own text nor the Judicial Council rules it references were fetched for this clause, so this clause does not state what form that assistance takes in a specific county, or whether it is confidential.
